You are under a false assumption that creating something gives it a certain value. That is not always true.

There is a difference between the physical goods and "emotional" goods if you want to call them that. A physical good is like milk - it has certain value to people, there is no way around that. You can't just copy milk, and if you steal milk, its theft. The price of milk is what you pay for the actual milk and the process that goes into creating it.

But an emotional good is different. So this is a little bit of a better example: suppose soldering irons have been invented, and people use them to solder whatever they want. However, you were fucking around with one, and notices that steel wool does a really good job of cleaning the iron tip. So you design a product that is essentially a little stand with some steel wool that people can use to clean the tip. And you release this for like $10 a piece, and people notice your product, but they also notice that they can just use steel wool that costs .99c for the same effect. So is every single person who saw your product, but decides to use the .99c piece of steel wool robbing you of $9.01?

Thats the issue with software - its an emotional good. You can't exactly steal emotional goods like that. A lot of the business world is built on capitalizing this fact, with patents and creating products at the right price point with added features that people are going to buy instead of finding cheaper alternatives.

And while it may seem that software is far from that, the fact that it takes a lot of man hours to create something aesthetically pleasing is irrelevant to the fact that its an emotional good - just an arrangement of bits on your hard drive. And if you ignore any laws surrounding software copyright (which a lot of people argue against actually, especially those that are in the field), then you find its really no different.
